I-46.explain: Amniotic fluid index (AFI) sums the deepest pocket in four quadrants; too much or too little signals a problem with fetal urine output or swallowing.

checks.q: Which AFI defines oligohydramnios?
checks.why: Oligohydramnios is AFI under 5 cm; polyhydramnios is AFI above 24-25 cm.

I-46.explain: Poly = fetus cannot swallow/absorb (atresias) or pees too much (diabetes); oligo = no urine made, urine blocked, or fluid leaking out.
I-46.hook: Oligo: no pee, blocked pee, leaking bag. ACEi/ARB shut fetal kidneys.

checks.q: Which maternal condition causes polyhydramnios via fetal osmotic diuresis?
checks.why: Maternal hyperglycaemia → fetal hyperglycaemia → osmotic diuresis → excess fluid. Pre-eclampsia tends to cause oligohydramnios.

checks.q: What is the commonest cause of oligohydramnios?
checks.why: Leakage from preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is the commonest cause; renal agenesis and PUV are rarer.

checks.q: Which drug class taken in pregnancy can cause oligohydramnios?
checks.why: ACEi/ARBs impair fetal renal perfusion and urine output, causing oligohydramnios; they are contraindicated in pregnancy.

I-46.explain: From mid-pregnancy the fetus makes fluid by urinating and removes it by swallowing; fluid in the airways is needed to stretch and grow the lungs.
I-46.hook: Fetus pees in, drinks out. No fluid, no lungs.

checks.q: After 20 weeks, what is the main source of amniotic fluid?
checks.why: Fetal urine dominates after 20 weeks; fetal swallowing removes it.

checks.q: What is the lethal consequence of early oligohydramnios?
checks.why: Without fluid the lungs fail to distend and grow → pulmonary hypoplasia, the usual cause of death.

I-46.explain: A stretched uterus contracts early and releases a gush when membranes rupture; too little fluid compresses the fetus and cord.
I-46.hook: Potter: Pulmonary hypoplasia, Odd face, Twisted limbs, Renal agenesis.

checks.q: After rapid decompression of polyhydramnios, which complication may occur?
checks.why: Sudden loss of uterine volume can shear the placenta off → abruption; cord prolapse and preterm labour also occur.

checks.q: Pulmonary hypoplasia, twisted facies and limb deformities form which sequence?
checks.why: Potter sequence results from oligohydramnios, classically from renal agenesis. Pierre Robin is micrognathia/glossoptosis.

checks.q: Besides growth restriction, what fetal complication does oligohydramnios cause in labour?
checks.why: Little fluid cushions the cord poorly → compression. Cord prolapse is a polyhydramnios risk.

I-46.explain: Ultrasound measures fluid and often reveals the cause: dilated stomach plus duodenum or a distended bladder with dilated posterior urethra.

checks.q: A keyhole bladder on prenatal ultrasound suggests what?
checks.why: Dilated bladder and posterior urethra form a keyhole in PUV; double bubble indicates duodenal atresia.

checks.q: Oligohydramnios before roughly which gestation causes the most severe lung hypoplasia?
checks.why: Fluid loss before ~24 weeks hits the canalicular phase of lung growth → most severe hypoplasia.

I-46.explain: Polyhydramnios may mean the baby cannot swallow, so test before feeding; for oligo, the lungs determine outcome.

checks.q: Newborn after polyhydramnios: what before the first feed?
checks.why: Passing an NG tube excludes oesophageal atresia before feeding risks aspiration.

checks.q: Which drug can reduce severe polyhydramnios?
checks.why: Indomethacin reduces fetal urine output; amnioreduction is the alternative. Mild term cases are managed expectantly.

checks.q: In oligohydramnios, what is the main cause of death?
checks.why: Pulmonary hypoplasia is the killer; management otherwise targets the cause.

I-47.explain: Newborns rarely have primary cardiac arrest; bradycardia is due to hypoxia, so inflating the lungs fixes the heart. A rising heart rate proves it works.
I-47.hook: Babies arrest from lungs, not hearts: aerate first.

checks.q: Newborn arrest is usually of what origin?
checks.why: Neonatal arrest is respiratory; aerating the lungs is the priority.

checks.q: Best indicator of successful newborn resuscitation?
checks.why: A rising heart rate is the best sign that ventilation is working; colour is unreliable.

I-47.explain: Hypoxic babies first stop breathing (primary apnoea), then gasp, then stop for good; post-dates babies pass meconium in utero.

checks.q: After primary apnoea and gasping, what follows in hypoxia?
checks.why: Hypoxia sequence: primary apnoea → gasping → terminal apnoea, which needs active ventilation.

checks.q: Meconium aspiration typically affects which infants?
checks.why: The mature gut passes meconium, so term and post-term infants are affected; preterms rarely.

I-47.explain: The first breaths replace lung fluid with air; oxygen dilates pulmonary vessels. Meconium blocks airways and inactivates surfactant.
I-47.hook: Slow heart in a baby = no oxygen until proven otherwise.

checks.q: Establishing FRC with the first breaths causes what?
checks.why: Lung aeration and oxygen drop pulmonary vascular resistance, switching to adult circulation.

checks.q: How does meconium impair lung function?
checks.why: Meconium inactivates surfactant and obstructs airways; neonatal bradycardia means hypoxia until proven otherwise.

I-47.explain: Initial assessment is quick: tone, breathing and heart rate decide whether to intervene; Apgar documents status but does not guide resuscitation.
I-47.hook: APGAR: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration.

checks.q: Below what heart rate should you intervene at birth?
checks.why: HR under 100 or not breathing → start inflation breaths; under 60 after effective ventilation → compressions.

checks.q: When is the Apgar score assessed?
checks.why: Apgar is scored at 1 and 5 minutes (repeated later if low).

I-47.explain: HR is heard with a stethoscope then monitored by ECG or right-hand (pre-ductal) oximetry; healthy newborns are blue at first, so saturations rise slowly.
I-47.hook: Sats climb slowly: ~70 at 3, ~80 at 5, ~90 at 10.

checks.q: What is the first tool to assess newborn heart rate?
checks.why: Stethoscope first, then ECG or pre-ductal SpO₂ for continuous monitoring.

checks.q: Target pre-ductal SpO₂ at 5 minutes after birth?
checks.why: Targets: 70-75% at 3 min, 80-85% at 5 min, 85-95% at 10 min.

checks.q: During PPV, the left chest transilluminates brighter. Diagnosis?
checks.why: Free air in the pleura glows brighter on transillumination → left pneumothorax.

I-47.explain: Keep warm, then long inflation breaths open fluid-filled lungs; compressions only once ventilation is effective and HR stays below 60.
I-47.hook: 5 long breaths in air; 3 compressions : 1 breath.

checks.q: How long is each newborn inflation breath?
checks.why: Five inflation breaths of 2-3 s each; term babies start in air (21%).

checks.q: Newborn compression-to-ventilation ratio?
checks.why: 3:1 when HR is under 60 after 30 s of effective ventilation; 15:2 is paediatric BLS.

checks.q: Dose of adrenaline via UVC in newborn resuscitation?
checks.why: Adrenaline 20 µg/kg (range 10-30) via UVC; HIE is then cooled to 33-34 °C for 72 h, starting within 6 h.

I-48.explain: Children rarely have primary cardiac events; arrest is the end-point of untreated hypoxia or shock, so outcome depends on how fast effective resuscitation starts.
I-48.hook: Kids' hearts stop last - fix air and circulation early.

checks.q: Paediatric cardiac arrest is usually the end result of what?
checks.why: Children arrest after progressive hypoxia or shock, unlike adults with primary cardiac causes.

checks.q: Key determinant of survival in paediatric arrest?
checks.why: Elapsed time to effective resuscitation is the key to survival.

I-48.explain: Failing breathing or circulation exhausts the child, hypoxia slows the heart and it ends in asystole, which is why non-shockable rhythms dominate.
I-48.hook: Hypoxia → brady → asystole: kids rarely need the defib.

checks.q: In the hypoxic arrest sequence, what precedes asystole?
checks.why: Respiratory failure/shock → tiring → hypoxia → bradycardia → asystole.

checks.q: Commonest arrest rhythms in children?
checks.why: Non-shockable rhythms (asystole, PEA) are commonest in paediatric arrest.

I-48.explain: With obstruction or tiring, the diaphragm pulls the abdomen out while the compliant chest is sucked in. PEA means electrical activity without output.
I-48.hook: Seesaw breathing: chest in, belly out.

checks.q: Paradoxical breathing: on inspiration, the chest moves how?
checks.why: Chest moves inward and abdomen outward during inhalation, and vice versa.

checks.q: Organised rhythm without a palpable pulse is called what?
checks.why: Pulseless electrical activity: organised electrical rhythm but no palpable pulse.

I-48.explain: ABCDE assessment looks for work of breathing, circulation and neurology systematically; never forget glucose.

checks.q: In the ABCDE assessment, which scale assesses disability quickly?
checks.why: AVPU (Alert, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) plus glucose assesses D in ABCDE.

I-48.explain: Oximeters read light absorption by Hb in pulsatile flow, so abnormal Hb, low Hb or poor perfusion fool them; they also say nothing about CO₂.
I-48.hook: Sats tell you O₂, not CO₂ - ventilation needs capnography.

checks.q: Pulse oximetry is unreliable in which poisoning?
checks.why: Carboxyhaemoglobin reads as oxyhaemoglobin → falsely normal SpO₂. Also methaemoglobinaemia, anaemia, cold extremities.

checks.q: To assess ventilation rather than oxygenation, use what?
checks.why: SpO₂ ignores ventilation; CO₂ requires capnography or a blood gas.

I-48.explain: Spontaneously breathing children get maximal oxygen via reservoir mask; in arrest, give rescue breaths first because the cause is hypoxic.
I-48.hook: 5 breaths, then 15:2; shock 4 J/kg; amio after shocks 3 and 5.

checks.q: Oxygen flow via reservoir mask for a conscious breathing child?
checks.why: Face mask with reservoir at high flow 10-15 l/min.

checks.q: Adrenaline dose in paediatric asystole/PEA?
checks.why: Adrenaline 10 µg/kg IV/IO every 3-5 min with CPR (15:2 after 5 rescue breaths).

checks.q: Shock energy for paediatric VF/pulseless VT?
checks.why: Unsynchronised 4 J/kg; amiodarone after the 3rd and 5th shocks.

I-49.explain: In fever the body deliberately resets its thermostat higher; in hyperthermia the set point is normal but heat overwhelms it.
I-49.hook: Fever = thermostat turned up, not a broken boiler.

checks.q: What is the mechanism of fever?
checks.why: Fever is a cytokine-driven rise in the hypothalamic set point; heat-loss failure is hyperthermia.

I-49.explain: Microbial products (pyrogens) trigger immune cells to release endogenous pyrogenic cytokines. Early neonatal sepsis reflects maternal flora acquired at birth.

checks.q: Which cytokines mediate fever?
checks.why: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α are endogenous pyrogens; IL-10/TGF-β are anti-inflammatory.

checks.q: Early-onset neonatal sepsis occurs within what time of birth?
checks.why: Early-onset is within 72 hours (some define 7 days); it reflects vertical transmission.

I-49.explain: Cytokines induce COX-2 to make PGE₂, which raises the set point; the body then conserves and generates heat. NSAIDs and paracetamol block this.
I-49.hook: Block COX → no PGE₂ → thermostat resets.

checks.q: Which mediator raises the hypothalamic set point?
checks.why: Cytokines induce hypothalamic PGE₂, raising the set point → shivering and vasoconstriction.

checks.q: How do antipyretics lower fever?
checks.why: Antipyretics inhibit COX, reducing PGE₂; fever itself is not harmful.

I-49.explain: Young infants have immature immunity and few signs, so any fever under 3 months is high risk; signs of poor perfusion or meningism are red.

checks.q: NICE: which temperature makes a child under 3 months red risk?
checks.why: Under 3 months with ≥ 38 °C is red; ≥ 39 °C at 3-6 months is amber.

checks.q: NICE amber: fever for how many days?
checks.why: Fever for 5 days or more is amber (consider Kawasaki disease).

I-49.explain: The traffic-light system stratifies febrile under-5s; neonates get full septic screen and rapid antibiotics. Pain scales match the child's ability to self-report.
I-49.hook: FLACC for babies, faces from 4, numbers from 8.

checks.q: NICE traffic light system applies to children of what age?
checks.why: The NICE traffic light system is for febrile children under 5; red features prompt septic work-up.

checks.q: In suspected neonatal sepsis, give antibiotics within what time?
checks.why: After blood culture (plus CRP, LP), antibiotics within 1 hour.

checks.q: Which pain scale suits a preverbal child?
checks.why: FLACC (behavioural) for preverbal; Wong-Baker from age 4; numeric from 8.

I-49.explain: Treat the child's distress, not the number. Aspirin risks Reye syndrome; codeine is unpredictable as ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers make excess morphine.

checks.q: Paracetamol dose for a febrile distressed child?
checks.why: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4-6 hourly; ibuprofen 10 mg/kg three times daily.

checks.q: Why is aspirin avoided under 16 years?
checks.why: Aspirin is linked to Reye syndrome; antipyretics also do not prevent febrile seizures.

checks.q: Empirical antibiotics for neonatal sepsis?
checks.why: Ampicillin + gentamicin covers GBS, E. coli and Listeria; codeine is contraindicated under 12 (CYP2D6).

I-50.explain: Shock means tissues get too little oxygen, regardless of blood pressure. Types follow the failing part: volume, vessels, pump, obstruction or oxygen carriage.
I-50.hook: Shock types: Hypo, Distributive, Cardiogenic, Obstructive, Dissociative.

checks.q: Shock from carbon monoxide or severe anaemia is which type?
checks.why: Dissociative shock: oxygen delivery fails despite flow because Hb cannot carry O₂.

I-50.explain: Fluid loss is commonest in children, but sepsis, anaphylaxis and cardiac causes matter. A duct-dependent lesion decompensates as the duct closes in the first weeks.
I-50.hook: Grey baby, 1-2 weeks, no femorals = duct closing.

checks.q: Commonest cause of hypovolaemic shock in children?
checks.why: Gastroenteritis with dehydration is the commonest; haemorrhage follows trauma.

checks.q: Neonate aged 1-2 weeks in shock, femoral pulses weaker than brachial: suggests?
checks.why: Duct closure in a duct-dependent systemic lesion (e.g. coarctation) causes shock with weak femorals.

I-50.explain: Children have strong vasoconstriction and rely on heart rate, holding BP until late; when BP falls, decompensation is imminent.

checks.q: Children maintain BP until roughly what volume is lost?
checks.why: Tachycardia + vasoconstriction compensate until 30-40% of volume is lost.

checks.q: In paediatric shock, hypotension is what kind of sign?
checks.why: Hypotension is late; tachycardia is the early sign.

I-50.explain: Compensated shock shows tachycardia and poor perfusion; once the heart slows and BP falls, the child is about to arrest.

checks.q: Earliest sign of shock in children?
checks.why: Tachycardia is earliest; CRT >2 s, mottling, oliguria and lactate follow.

checks.q: Bradycardia with hypotension in a shocked child means what?
checks.why: Bradycardia + hypotension indicates decompensation and imminent arrest.

I-50.explain: Baseline cultures and gases guide treatment. Expected minimum systolic BP rises with age. Reassessment after boluses detects fluid overload.

checks.q: Which test reflects tissue hypoperfusion in shock?
checks.why: Raised lactate indicates anaerobic metabolism from poor perfusion; take cultures, gas, glucose too.

checks.q: Hypotension threshold in a child aged 1-10 years?
checks.why: Hypotension: systolic below 70 + (2 × age) mmHg in 1-10 year olds.

checks.q: After each fluid bolus, a new enlarged liver edge suggests what?
checks.why: Liver enlargement or crackles after boluses signal fluid overload; reassess HR, CRT, BP each time.

I-50.explain: Restore volume fast and treat infection early; if fluids fail, add vasoactive drugs. Clindamycin halts toxin production; IM adrenaline is always first in anaphylaxis.

checks.q: Fluid bolus volume in paediatric septic shock?
checks.why: Official answer: 20 ml/kg, antibiotics within 1 hour. (Newer ERC/APLS: 10 ml/kg aliquots - exam wants 20.)

checks.q: Why add clindamycin in toxic shock syndrome?
checks.why: Clindamycin inhibits ribosomal toxin synthesis; fluid-refractory shock needs adrenaline or noradrenaline.

checks.q: First drug in paediatric anaphylaxis?
checks.why: IM adrenaline first (150 µg under 6 years); steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts.

I-51.explain: Birth injuries are classified by the tissue layer bleeding (scalp swellings) or by the nerve roots stretched (plexus palsies).
I-51.hook: Layer for scalp, root for arm.

checks.q: Scalp birth injuries are classified by what?
checks.why: Caput, cephalhaematoma and subgaleal bleeds differ by anatomical layer; plexus injuries by nerve root.

I-51.explain: Big babies and instrumental or obstructed deliveries apply more force; maternal glucose drives fetal insulin, a growth hormone in utero.
I-51.hook: Sugar mum → big baby → stuck shoulders.

checks.q: Which is a major risk factor for neonatal birth injury?
checks.why: Shoulder dystocia, macrosomia, vacuum and forceps raise birth injury risk.

checks.q: Maternal hyperglycaemia leads to which fetal finding?
checks.why: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia promotes growth → macrosomia → birth trauma.

I-51.explain: Caput is oedema above the periosteum so it crosses sutures; cephalhaematoma is under periosteum, bounded by sutures; subgaleal space is huge, allowing massive bleeding.
I-51.hook: Caput crosses, cephal can't; subgaleal swallows blood.

checks.q: Which scalp swelling crosses suture lines?
checks.why: Caput (scalp oedema) crosses sutures; subperiosteal cephalhaematoma does not.

checks.q: Subgaleal haemorrhage results from injury to which vessels?
checks.why: Emissary veins rupture into the space between aponeurosis and periosteum.

checks.q: Erb palsy is caused by what mechanism?
checks.why: Lateral traction on the neck stretches C5-C6; arm hyperabduction gives Klumpke.

I-51.explain: Bleeds release haem that becomes bilirubin; subgaleal bleeds can hold a large blood volume. Root level determines the limb posture.

checks.q: Cephalhaematoma resorption can cause what?
checks.why: Breakdown of the collected blood increases bilirubin load → jaundice.

checks.q: Subgaleal haemorrhage typically follows what delivery?
checks.why: Vacuum extraction is the classic cause; it can lead to hypovolaemic shock.

checks.q: Klumpke palsy with Horner syndrome involves which roots?
checks.why: Klumpke = C8-T1 (claw hand, ± Horner via T1 sympathetics); Erb = C5-C6.

I-51.explain: Subgaleal blood loss shows as an enlarging head and falling Hb. The phrenic nerve shares roots with Erb, and the clavicle lies over vessels and plexus.

checks.q: How is a subgaleal haemorrhage monitored?
checks.why: Serial head circumference and Hb detect ongoing blood loss.

checks.q: Erb palsy with tachypnoea suggests which nerve injury?
checks.why: Phrenic nerve (C3-C5) palsy → diaphragm paralysis → tachypnoea.

checks.q: With a clavicle fracture, which structure also needs checking?
checks.why: The subclavian artery and brachial plexus lie beneath the clavicle.

I-51.explain: McRoberts flattens the sacral promontory; suprapubic pressure dislodges the shoulder. Most injuries heal, but persisting biceps weakness implies root avulsion.

checks.q: First manoeuvre in shoulder dystocia?
checks.why: McRoberts (hip flexion) + suprapubic pressure; fundal pressure worsens impaction.

checks.q: Commonest birth fracture?
checks.why: The clavicle is commonest and heals rapidly; 80% of plexus palsies resolve within 3 months.

checks.q: No biceps recovery by 3-6 months in Erb palsy: next step?
checks.why: Absent biceps recovery by 3-6 months warrants surgery; subgaleal bleeds need volume and blood.

I-52.explain: Curious toddlers ingest what they find, usually small amounts; adolescents take deliberate, often mixed overdoses.

checks.q: Accidental ingestion peaks at what age?
checks.why: Toddlers 1-4 y ingest accidentally; adolescents deliberately.

I-52.explain: Household medicines and products dominate; button batteries burn tissue. Lead paint was banned in 1978, so older homes are the source.

checks.q: Lead poisoning risk relates to homes built before which year?
checks.why: Lead-based paint was banned in 1978; older homes carry risk.

checks.q: Which ingested object needs urgent attention due to tissue burns?
checks.why: Button batteries cause electrical/caustic burns rapidly; other blunt objects usually pass.

I-52.explain: Paracetamol injury begins when glutathione runs out and NAPQI binds liver proteins. TCAs block cardiac sodium channels, slowing conduction.
I-52.hook: NAPQI eats glutathione; TCA widens QRS.

checks.q: Toxic metabolite of paracetamol?
checks.why: NAPQI is detoxified by glutathione until stores are exhausted → hepatotoxicity.

checks.q: Why do TCAs widen the QRS?
checks.why: TCAs block fast Na⁺ channels → wide QRS; iron is corrosive then a mitochondrial poison.

I-52.explain: Recognising the toxidrome points to the drug class. Paracetamol looks harmless early; aspirin first stimulates breathing, then causes acidosis.
I-52.hook: Pinpoint pupils = opioid; aspirin: alkalosis then acidosis.

checks.q: Pinpoint pupils indicate which toxidrome?
checks.why: Opioids cause miosis; anticholinergic and sympathomimetic toxidromes cause mydriasis.

checks.q: How does paracetamol overdose look on day 1?
checks.why: Day 1 is near asymptomatic - hence the need for levels; lead shows a blue gum line.

checks.q: Early acid-base change in aspirin poisoning?
checks.why: Salicylates stimulate respiration first → respiratory alkalosis; later mixed with metabolic acidosis.

I-52.explain: Stabilise first and calculate the worst-case dose. Paracetamol levels before 4 h are unreliable because absorption is incomplete.
I-52.hook: Paracetamol level at 4 h, plot on nomogram.

checks.q: Paracetamol level is plotted on the nomogram from what time?
checks.why: From 4 hours post-ingestion, when absorption is complete; iron gets X-ray + serum iron.

checks.q: How is ingested dose estimated in a child?
checks.why: Calculate in mg/kg and assume worst case; ABCDE + glucose first.

checks.q: Raised capillary lead level: next test?
checks.why: Capillary samples may be contaminated → confirm with venous lead level.

I-52.explain: Vomiting risks aspiration and caustic re-exposure. Charcoal binds most drugs early, not ions or alcohols. Antidotes target each mechanism.
I-52.hook: Charcoal won't bind: Iron, Lithium, Alcohols (ILA).

checks.q: Activated charcoal does not bind which substance?
checks.why: Charcoal does not bind iron, lithium or alcohols; use only within 1 hour; never induce vomiting.

checks.q: Antidote for iron poisoning?
checks.why: Desferrioxamine chelates iron; NAC for paracetamol, bicarbonate for TCA, naloxone for opioid.

checks.q: Button battery lodged in oesophagus: management?
checks.why: Oesophageal battery or coin needs urgent endoscopy; lead: DMSA if moderate, dimercaprol + EDTA if severe.

I-53.explain: Maltreatment covers acts (physical, sexual, emotional) and omissions; neglect is the most frequent although least visible.

checks.q: Commonest form of child maltreatment?
checks.why: Neglect is the commonest form of maltreatment.

I-53.explain: Abuse repeats across generations, usually by the main carer. Inconsolable crying peaks at 2-4 months, triggering shaking.

checks.q: Most significant parental risk factor for child abuse?
checks.why: A history of being abused is the strongest parental risk factor; abuser usually the primary caregiver.

checks.q: Peak age of shaken baby syndrome?
checks.why: Under 1 year, peaking at 2-4 months (crying peak); sexual abuse peaks at 9-12 years.

I-53.explain: Acceleration-deceleration shears veins bridging cortex to dura, and the vitreous tugs the retina; squeezing the chest levers the ribs posteriorly.
I-53.hook: Shake → bridging veins tear; grip → back ribs crack.

checks.q: Shaking causes subdural haemorrhage by tearing which vessels?
checks.why: Bridging veins tear → subdural; middle meningeal artery → epidural.

checks.q: Which fractures result from gripping the infant's chest?
checks.why: Squeezing levers ribs over transverse processes → posterior rib fractures.

I-53.explain: Red flags are history mismatch and patterns impossible accidentally: bruises before cruising, immersion scald lines.
I-53.hook: Those who don't cruise rarely bruise.

checks.q: Which history feature raises suspicion of abuse?
checks.why: Delay, changing story and injuries not fitting development suggest abuse.

checks.q: Which scald pattern suggests abuse?
checks.why: Forced immersion leaves sharp demarcation; any bruise in a non-mobile infant is also suspicious.

checks.q: Abusive head trauma triad: subdural, retinal haemorrhages and what?
checks.why: The triad is subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages and encephalopathy.

I-53.explain: Imaging shows bleeds, a repeat skeletal survey catches healing fractures missed initially; coagulation excludes mimics.

checks.q: When is the skeletal survey repeated?
checks.why: Repeat at 11-14 days reveals healing fractures not visible initially.

checks.q: Most specific fracture for abuse?
checks.why: Posterior rib and classic metaphyseal (corner) fractures are most specific.

I-53.explain: Protect the child: inform child protective services, document precisely, admit if unsafe; child welfare overrides confidentiality.

checks.q: First step when abuse is suspected?
checks.why: Contact child protective services; both abuse and neglect are reported.

checks.q: Welfare of the child overrides what?
checks.why: Child welfare overrides confidentiality; document exactly and admit if needed.

I-54.explain: An aspirated foreign body can lodge at any airway level; site determines symptoms, from stridor to unilateral wheeze.

checks.q: Airway foreign body may lodge where?
checks.why: An inhaled object sits in larynx, trachea or bronchus; oesophageal objects are swallowed, not aspirated.

I-54.explain: Toddlers lack molars to grind food and eat while moving; the right main bronchus is wider and more in line with the trachea.

checks.q: Peak age for airway foreign bodies?
checks.why: Toddlers 1-3 y: no molars, eat while running; nuts are classic.

checks.q: Why is the right lung most commonly affected?
checks.why: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.

I-54.explain: Partial obstruction lets air in on inspiration but not out (bronchi narrow on expiration) → hyperinflation. Complete obstruction absorbs distal air.

checks.q: Partial bronchial obstruction causes what on expiration?
checks.why: A check-valve effect traps air on expiration → hyperinflation.

checks.q: Complete bronchial obstruction leads to what?
checks.why: Distal air is absorbed → atelectasis; nuts are radiolucent so often not seen.

I-54.explain: After the choking episode, symptoms can settle for days, so a quiet child doesn't exclude it; later localised signs and infection appear.

checks.q: Bronchial foreign body classically causes which wheeze?
checks.why: Unilateral wheeze after a symptom-free interval, with recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe.

checks.q: Laryngotracheal foreign body presents with what?
checks.why: Upper airway obstruction gives stridor and cyanosis.

I-54.explain: Air trapping shifts the mediastinum with each breath; comparing inspiratory and expiratory films shows it. Radiolucent objects mean a normal X-ray proves nothing.
I-54.hook: Holzknecht = mediastinum swinging like a pendulum.

checks.q: Holzknecht sign indicates what?
checks.why: Official answer: pendulum mediastinal movement = airway foreign body aspiration.

checks.q: Which imaging helps diagnose an airway foreign body?
checks.why: Expiratory and inspiratory radiographs or fluoroscopy; a normal X-ray never excludes it.

I-54.explain: Infant livers and abdomens are vulnerable, so back blows and chest thrusts are used under 1; abdominal thrusts after. Rigid bronchoscopy is definitive.
I-54.hook: Under 1: back + chest. Over 1: back + tummy.

checks.q: Choking infant under 1 year: after 5 back blows give?
checks.why: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts risk liver injury in infants.

checks.q: Choking child over 1 year: which thrusts?
checks.why: Over 1 year, abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) after back blows.

checks.q: Definitive treatment of airway foreign body?
checks.why: Rigid bronchoscopy; a symptomatic swallowed coin needs emergency endoscopy.

I-55.explain: Every scan must be justified and use the lowest dose; prefer methods without ionising radiation such as ultrasound and MRI.
I-55.hook: ALARA: As Low As Reasonably Achievable.

checks.q: Radiation principle in paediatric imaging?
checks.why: ALARA: justification, optimisation and non-ionising methods first.

I-55.explain: Rapidly dividing cells are more DNA-damage prone, and children have decades for cancer to develop.

checks.q: Why are children more radiosensitive than adults?
options: Dividing cells and longer remaining life
checks.why: Dividing cells, longer life ahead and organs close to the beam increase risk.

I-55.explain: The open fontanelle is an acoustic window; blood reflects echoes while CSF is black. The germinal matrix is fragile and vascular in preterms.
I-55.hook: Fontanelle = window; germinal matrix = preterm bleed site.

checks.q: Cranial ultrasound in infants is done through what?
checks.why: The anterior fontanelle provides the acoustic window; blood is echogenic, CSF anechoic.

checks.q: Preterm intraventricular haemorrhage arises where?
checks.why: The fragile germinal matrix is the source of preterm IVH.

I-55.explain: The thymus is large in infants and shrinks later; absence suggests T-cell immunodeficiency. A normal thymus is soft and does not compress the trachea.
I-55.hook: Sail sign until 3; no sail = DiGeorge/SCID.

checks.q: Thymus shadow is normally visible on CXR until what age?
checks.why: Official answer: till 3 years; absence suggests DiGeorge or SCID.

checks.q: Mediastinal shadow narrowing the trachea suggests what?
checks.why: Normal thymus is soft and doesn't compress the trachea; narrowing means a mass.

I-55.explain: Ultrasound first, MRI next; for urinary tract: anatomy (US), reflux (MCUG), scars (DMSA, delayed so acute inflammation resolves), drainage (MAG3).

checks.q: Cranial ultrasound best detects which conditions?
checks.why: Official answer: brain haemorrhage and hydrocephalus.

checks.q: When is DMSA done after UTI to show scars?
checks.why: DMSA 4-6 months after infection so acute changes don't mimic scars.

I-55.explain: Speed wins in trauma (CT); stroke often needs MRI; ultrasound suits pyloric stenosis and intussusception; bilious vomiting needs contrast for malrotation.
I-55.hook: Green vomit → upper GI contrast for malrotation.

checks.q: Imaging for a polytraumatised child?
checks.why: Exam answer: polytrauma → acute CT (in practice selective); head trauma: non-contrast CT if GCS ≤ 14 or skull fracture.

checks.q: Suspected stroke with normal CT: next imaging?
checks.why: CT misses early ischaemia; MRI/MRA is needed.

checks.q: Imaging for bilious vomiting in an infant?
checks.why: Upper GI contrast to rule out malrotation; ultrasound for pyloric stenosis and intussusception.

II-1.explain: Vaccines train the immune system without disease, creating memory B and T cells that rapidly make high-affinity IgG on real exposure.

checks.q: Vaccines protect by priming what?
checks.why: Memory B and T cells produce fast, high-affinity IgG on infection.

II-1.explain: Live attenuated vaccines replicate, so they can harm a fetus or an immunodeficient (SCID) child. Hungary's schedule includes newborn BCG.
II-1.hook: Live: MMR, Varicella, Rotavirus, BCG - not in SCID or pregnancy.

checks.q: Which vaccine is live attenuated?
checks.why: Live: MMR, varicella, rotavirus, BCG - avoid in SCID and pregnancy.

checks.q: In Hungary, BCG is given to whom?
checks.why: Hungary vaccinates all newborns with BCG; varicella mandatory since 2019.

II-1.explain: Maternal IgG neutralises live measles vaccine in early infancy. Polysaccharides are T-independent, so infants respond poorly unless conjugated to protein.

checks.q: Why is MMR given after 12 months?
checks.why: Residual maternal antibodies neutralise the live vaccine earlier.

checks.q: Why do conjugate vaccines work in infants?
checks.why: Protein carrier converts a T-independent polysaccharide response into T-dependent.

II-1.explain: Live vaccines replicate briefly, so mild disease-like symptoms appear after the incubation period.
II-1.hook: MMR rash a week later, not a day.

checks.q: When do MMR fever and rash appear after vaccination?
checks.why: After viral replication: 7-12 days post-vaccination.

checks.q: A few-lesion rash after varicella vaccine reflects what?
checks.why: Mild rash with few lesions = vaccine-strain replication.

II-1.explain: True contraindications are few; minor illness and prematurity are not reasons to delay. Pertussis is held after encephalopathy.
II-1.hook: Only anaphylaxis stops all; preterms go by birthday.

checks.q: The only universal vaccine contraindication?
options: Anaphylaxis to previous dose or component
checks.why: Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is the only universal contraindication.

checks.q: After DTaP encephalopathy, what is withheld?
checks.why: Encephalopathy → hold pertussis; anaphylaxis → no future DTaP doses.

checks.q: Preterm infants are vaccinated according to which age?
checks.why: Preterms follow chronological age; mild illness is not a contraindication.

II-1.explain: Infant series at 2-4-6 months; live MMR/varicella after maternal antibody wanes, with a booster; adolescent boosters and HPV before sexual exposure.

checks.q: Hepatitis B vaccine schedule?
checks.why: Hep B at birth, 2 and 6 months; DTaP, IPV, PCV15, rotavirus at 2, 4, 6 months.

checks.q: MMR and varicella are given at which ages?
checks.why: MMR and varicella at 1 and 4 years; annual influenza from 6 months.

checks.q: Which vaccines are given at age 11?
checks.why: Age 11: Tdap, meningococcal and HPV (HPV through 26).

II-2.explain: Development is assessed across separate domains because a child can be delayed in one and normal in others.

checks.q: Which is one of the four developmental domains?
checks.why: Domains: gross motor, fine motor/vision, speech/hearing, social.

II-2.explain: Regression suggests neurodegenerative or serious disease; early handedness implies weakness of the other side, e.g. hemiplegic CP.
II-2.hook: Early hand preference = the other hand is weak.

checks.q: Which developmental finding is an urgent red flag?
checks.why: Any loss of skills (regression) is urgent; walking at 15 months is normal.

checks.q: Hand preference is a red flag before what age?
checks.why: Hand preference before 12 months suggests weakness of the other side (e.g. hemiplegia).

II-2.explain: Myelination proceeds head-to-tail and centre-to-periphery, so head control precedes sitting and walking; cortical maturation suppresses primitive reflexes.
II-2.hook: Head to toe, core to fingers.

checks.q: Developmental progression follows which direction?
checks.why: Myelination drives cephalocaudal, proximal→distal progression.

checks.q: Primitive reflexes normally persist until what age?
checks.why: Official answer: till 6-12 months; persistence suggests UMN lesion (e.g. CP).

II-2.explain: Milestones follow a predictable order; memorise the anchor ages and judge a child against the upper limit, not the average.
II-2.hook: Smile 6 wk, roll 6 mo, sit 9 mo, walk 12-18 mo.

checks.q: Normal age of social smile?
checks.why: Social smile at 6 weeks; lifts head at 2 months, rolls at 6 months.

checks.q: Sitting alone and stranger anxiety appear at about what age?
checks.why: Sits alone and stranger anxiety at 9 months; pulls to stand at 9-12 months.

checks.q: Upper limit for independent walking?
checks.why: Walks at 12-18 months; not walking by 18 months needs assessment.

II-2.explain: Single measurements mislead; serial centile plots show trajectory. Undernutrition hits weight first, then length, and head last.

checks.q: Growth failure: crossing how many major centile lines?
checks.why: Weight below 5th centile or crossing two major lines defines growth failure.

checks.q: In failure to thrive, which falls first?
checks.why: Weight falls first, then height, then head circumference (brain spared).

checks.q: What matters most when interpreting centile charts?
checks.why: Judge the trajectory of serial weight, length and head circumference.

II-2.explain: Babies lose weight initially, regain it, then grow fast; serial growth velocity detects problems earlier than absolute size.
II-2.hook: Weight: back at 2 wk, ×2 at 4-5 mo, ×3 at 1 yr.

checks.q: Birth weight triples by what age?
checks.why: Regained by 2 weeks, doubles by 4-5 months, triples by 12 months.

checks.q: Most sensitive marker of growth?
checks.why: Growth velocity is most sensitive; length rises 50% by 1 year.

II-3.explain: Normal term newborn reference values anchor everything; SGA is a statistical definition (below 10th centile), unlike FGR which implies pathology.
II-3.hook: Term: 2.5-4 kg, head 35 cm; SGA below 10th.

checks.q: Normal term birth weight range?
checks.why: Term birth weight 2500-4000 g, head circumference ~35 cm.

checks.q: SGA is birth weight below which centile?
checks.why: Small for gestational age = below the 10th centile for gestation.

II-3.explain: Smoking constricts placental vessels and causes hypoxia. Late placental problems spare the head; early fetal causes restrict everything.

checks.q: Leading cause of low birth weight in developed countries?
checks.why: Smoking is the leading cause of LBW in developed countries.

checks.q: Asymmetric FGR is usually due to what?
checks.why: Asymmetric = placental insufficiency; trisomies and TORCH cause symmetric growth lag.

II-3.explain: With late placental failure, blood is redirected to the brain (head sparing); hypoxia drives erythropoietin, making thick blood.

checks.q: Asymmetric FGR spares which part?
checks.why: Late placental FGR redistributes flow to the brain → head spared; symmetric = global lag.

checks.q: Chronic fetal hypoxia leads to polycythaemia above what haematocrit?
checks.why: Hypoxia → EPO → haematocrit over 65% → hyperviscosity, jaundice.

II-3.explain: IUGR babies have small glycogen and fat stores; preterms show immature skin, ears and tone, and immature lungs, brain vessels, gut and retina.
II-3.hook: Preterm problems: RDS, IVH, PDA, NEC, ROP.

checks.q: Typical metabolic problem in IUGR newborns?
checks.why: Low glycogen stores → hypoglycaemia; also hypothermia and polycythaemia.

checks.q: Which feature suggests prematurity?
checks.why: Preterm: thin red skin, lanugo, soft ears, hypotonia; deep creases mean maturity.

checks.q: Respiratory distress syndrome in preterms is due to what?
checks.why: RDS = surfactant deficiency; retained fluid is transient tachypnoea.

II-3.explain: Weight categories step down by 500 g; gestation comes from early ultrasound or Ballard exam. Absent end-diastolic flow means high placental resistance.

checks.q: Very low birth weight is under what?
checks.why: LBW < 2500 g, VLBW < 1500 g, ELBW < 1000 g.

checks.q: Postnatal gestational age assessment uses which score?
checks.why: New Ballard score (or dating ultrasound) estimates gestation.

checks.q: Absent/reversed umbilical end-diastolic flow in FGR means what?
checks.why: Absent or reversed EDF signals severe placental resistance → urgent delivery.

II-3.explain: Antenatal steroids mature lungs, MgSO₄ protects the brain; surfactant replaces what is missing. NEC needs gut rest; ROP is lasered.

checks.q: Antenatal glucocorticoids are given at which gestation?
checks.why: Maternal steroids at 24-34 weeks + MgSO₄; artificial surfactant after birth.

checks.q: First-line management of NEC?
options: NPO, NG tube, IV fluids, antibiotics
checks.why: NPO, NG decompression, fluids, antibiotics; surgery for perforation.

checks.q: Treatment of retinopathy of prematurity?
checks.why: ROP is treated with laser photocoagulation.

II-4.explain: Supply matches demand, so feed whenever the baby wants; breast milk alone covers needs for 6 months.
II-4.hook: On demand, 6 months exclusive, 2 years total.

checks.q: How often should a baby be breastfed?
checks.why: Official answer: on demand; exclusively for 6 months, continue to 2 years.

II-4.explain: Galactosaemic infants cannot metabolise lactose; some maternal infections transmit via milk or close contact. Hep B is covered by vaccine and immunoglobulin.
II-4.hook: Galactosaemia, HIV, TB, varicella: no breast. Hep B, mastitis: fine.

checks.q: Which infant condition contraindicates breastfeeding?
checks.why: Galactosaemia is an absolute contraindication; PKU allows partial breastfeeding.

checks.q: Which maternal condition is NOT a contraindication?
checks.why: Hepatitis B and mastitis are not contraindications; HIV, untreated TB, varicella are.

II-4.explain: Prolactin makes milk, oxytocin ejects it; emptying drives production. Lower protein suits immature kidneys; colostrum gives passive IgA.

checks.q: Which hormone causes milk let-down?
checks.why: Oxytocin ejects milk; prolactin drives synthesis.

checks.q: Breast milk protein content compared with cow's milk?
checks.why: Official answer: one third; colostrum is rich in IgA.

II-4.explain: Wet nappies show intake; early weight loss up to 10% is normal, regained by 2 weeks. Breast milk jaundice is from a milk enzyme deconjugating bilirubin.

checks.q: Adequate feeding at day 5: how many wet nappies daily?
checks.why: ≥ 5 wet nappies daily at 5 days; weight loss up to 10% is acceptable.

checks.q: Birth weight is regained by what age?
checks.why: Birth weight is regained by 2 weeks.

checks.q: Which milk enzyme causes breast milk jaundice?
checks.why: β-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin → enterohepatic reabsorption.

II-4.explain: Cow's milk is iron-poor, causes occult GI bleeding and has a high solute load. Infants need far more energy and fluid per kg than adults.
II-4.hook: 100 kcal and 150 ml per kg per day.

checks.q: Cow's milk should first be given after what age?
checks.why: Official answer: after 12 months, otherwise iron deficiency and renal solute load.

checks.q: Early infant energy requirement?
checks.why: About 100-110 kcal/kg/day; fluid about 150 ml/kg/day.

checks.q: Oedema and swollen abdomen indicate which malnutrition?
checks.why: Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency) causes oedema; marasmus is wasting.

II-4.explain: Solids at ~6 months, never before 17 weeks; honey may contain botulinum spores. Breastfeeding jaundice is underfeeding; milk jaundice is benign.

checks.q: Why no honey under 12 months?
checks.why: Honey may carry C. botulinum spores → infant botulism; solids not before 17 weeks.

checks.q: Management of breastfeeding jaundice?
checks.why: It reflects underfeeding → feed more often (q2h); breast milk jaundice: continue.

checks.q: Routine vitamin D supplement for infants?
checks.why: Vitamin D 400 IU daily for all, plus vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth.

II-5.explain: Psychosomatic symptoms are genuinely felt, driven by stress rather than disease. Bulimia needs recurrent binges plus compensation at a set frequency.

checks.q: Commonest psychosomatic complaint in children?
checks.why: Functional abdominal pain is the commonest psychosomatic condition.

checks.q: Bulimia: binge + compensation at what minimum frequency?
checks.why: DSM-5: at least weekly for 3 months.

II-5.explain: Psychosocial stress at school or home triggers symptoms; anxiety about leaving a parent can present as school refusal.
II-5.hook: Tummy ache on school mornings = separation anxiety.

checks.q: School avoidance is typically linked to what?
checks.why: Separation anxiety commonly underlies school avoidance.

checks.q: Anorexia nervosa peaks in which group?
checks.why: Anorexia peaks in adolescent girls.

II-5.explain: Stress activates the HPA and brain-gut axis, amplifying gut sensation. Starvation switches off pulsatile GnRH. Vomiting loses acid and volume, triggering aldosterone.

checks.q: Functional pain arises via the brain-gut axis causing what?
checks.why: Stress → HPA and brain-gut axis → visceral hypersensitivity.

checks.q: Amenorrhoea in anorexia results from loss of what?
checks.why: Loss of pulsatile GnRH → low LH/FSH/oestrogen → amenorrhoea.

checks.q: Recurrent vomiting causes HCl loss and raised what?
checks.why: Volume loss activates aldosterone → renal K⁺ loss and alkalosis.

II-5.explain: Starvation slows the body; purging damages teeth and glands and calluses knuckles. Conversion patients may seem unconcerned by dramatic deficits.
II-5.hook: Russell = knuckle scars from fingers in throat.

checks.q: Cardiovascular sign typical of anorexia nervosa?
checks.why: AN: bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo, amenorrhoea, MVP.

checks.q: Knuckle calluses in bulimia are called what?
checks.why: Russell sign from induced vomiting; also parotid hypertrophy and enamel erosion.

checks.q: La belle indifférence is typical of which disorder?
checks.why: Unconcern about symptoms (la belle indifférence) suggests conversion disorder.

II-5.explain: Look for red flags, then stop testing - excessive investigation reinforces illness. Vomiting yields low K⁺ and Cl⁻ with alkalosis. Admit AN when physiology is unstable.
II-5.hook: AN admission: HR under 40, SBP under 80.

checks.q: In psychosomatic complaints, after excluding red flags, what next?
checks.why: Exclude red flags but avoid endless tests, which reinforce illness.

checks.q: Typical acid-base finding in bulimia?
checks.why: Vomiting causes hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.

checks.q: Anorexia admission criterion for heart rate?
checks.why: Notes: admit if HR under 40, SBP under 80, temp under 35.5 °C, %mBMI under 70%, syncope (SAHM uses HR under 50).

II-5.explain: Families are central to adolescent AN recovery; bulimia responds to CBT ± fluoxetine. Refeeding drives insulin, shifting phosphate into cells.

checks.q: First-line treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa?
checks.why: Family-based therapy is first-line; bulimia uses psychotherapy ± fluoxetine.

checks.q: Key electrolyte disturbance in refeeding syndrome?
checks.why: Insulin surge drives phosphate into cells → hypophosphataemia.

checks.q: Managing persistent somatic symptoms involves what?
checks.why: Regular monthly visits with one physician and screening for self-harm.
